text: Evi Nemeth (born June 7, 1940 – missing-at-sea June or July 2013) was an engineer, author, and teacher renowned for her expertise in computer system administration and networks. She was the lead author of the "bibles" of system administration: UNIX System Administration Handbook (1989, 1995, 2000), Linux Administration Handbook (2002, 2006), and UNIX and Linux System Administration Handbook (2010, 2017). Known in technology circles as the matriarch of system administration, she earned her bachelor's degree in mathematics from Penn State in 1961 and her PhD in mathematics from the University of Waterloo, Ontario in 1971. She taught at Florida Atlantic University and the State University of New York at Utica (SUNY Tech) before joining the computer science department at the University of Colorado Boulder (CU-Boulder) in 1980, where she served as manager of the college's computing facility from 1982 to 1986. She also held visiting Associate Professor positions at Dartmouth College in 1990 and UC San Diego in 1998, while on sabbatical from CU-Boulder. At CU-Boulder, she was well known for her undergraduate systems administration program, which enabled students to gain in-depth knowledge and skills in Unix system administration. Together with Steve Wozniak, she established the Woz scholarship program at CU-Boulder to fund inquisitive undergraduates. Nemeth was also recognized for her ability to inspire and teach young people, mentoring numerous middle- and high-school students—known as "the munchkins"—and talented young undergraduates, who worked with her to support computing at the university and attended national meetings where they installed networks and broadcast sessions on the Internet via the multicast backbone. She coached the university's student programming teams in the ACM International Collegiate Programming Contest. From 1998 to 2006, she worked with the Cooperative Association for Internet Data Analysis (CAIDA) at the University of California, San Diego, on Internet measurement and visualization projects. Outside the United States, she contributed to bringing Internet technology to the developing world through programs of the Internet Society and the United Nations Development Programme. A network guru T-shirt from the 1980s, featuring OSI Model layers with an added "financial" Layer 8 and a "political" Layer 9, was credited to her. During the Summer 1994 USENIX conference in Boston, she coordinated the production of a commemorative deck of playing cards celebrating the 25th anniversary of UNIX. After retiring, she sailed her 40-foot sailboat Wonderland around the world, including a circuit of the Atlantic, through the Panama Canal, and across the Pacific to New Zealand. In late May 2013, she traveled with six others aboard the vintage yacht Niña across the Tasman Sea en route to Australia from New Zealand. On June 4, the last message sent by Nemeth from Niña was received, as the Tasman Sea had 65 mile-per-hour winds and swell height reaching 26 feet; a natural disaster (e.g., a rogue wave) may have caused the boat’s disappearance. On July 5, New Zealand authorities officially ended the search for the Niña, though relatives of the crew continued to search.
